report:
## Research Report: Does Saw Palmetto Improve BPH Symptoms Long-Term vs. Placebo?

**Conclusion: No** — the weight of rigorous, long-term evidence indicates saw palmetto is not more effective than placebo for treating BPH symptoms.

**Evidence:**

1. **NEJM 2006 trial (STEP study)** — A one-year, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial found saw palmetto was "not superior to placebo for improving urinary symptoms and objective measures of benign prostatic hyperplasia," using standard doses in men with moderate-to-severe symptoms (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085).

2. **CAMUS trial (JAMA 2011)** — This larger, 72-week North American multicenter trial tested saw palmetto at up to three times the standard dose (escalating from 320mg to 960mg) against placebo. Even at these higher doses, saw palmetto did not reduce lower urinary tract symptoms more than placebo (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439).

3. **Cochrane Systematic Review (updated 2012, BJU International)** — This meta-analysis pooling multiple randomized controlled trials concluded that "Serenoa repens is no more effective than placebo in relieving urinary symptoms associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia," though it noted the herb is relatively safe with few side effects (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20941857/).

4. **Clinical summary (AAFP/Cochrane synopsis)** — A subsequent review of the Cochrane evidence reinforces this conclusion, noting saw palmetto does not meaningfully reduce LUTS compared to placebo (https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/0500/cochrane-saw-palmetto-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia).

**Summary:** While earlier, smaller, and often industry-funded studies suggested modest benefit, the largest and most rigorous placebo-controlled trials (STEP, CAMUS) and the Cochrane systematic reviews consistently find no significant long-term benefit of saw palmetto over placebo for BPH symptoms, even at higher doses. This evolution of evidence—from early promise to null results in better-designed studies—supports concluding "no."
